newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Trinidad sees petroleum industry revival.
newsitem.headline: Trinidad sees petroleum industry revival.

text.p: Trinidad and Tobago is experiencing a revival in its petroleum industry, with $5 billion in investments planned for the next five years and plenty of new opportunities for foreign companies, top officials said on Wednesday.

The government is currently evaluating 15 bids it received for four offshore exploration blocks, and is planning another licensing round for joint-ventures before the end of the year, said Donald Baldeosingh, president of state oil company Petrotrin.

Speaking at a conference here, he said Trinidad's crude oil production has fallen to 130,000 barrels per day (bpd) from its 1978 peak of 278,000 bpd, but new exploration using modern technology from foreign partners could revive it.
Trinidad's upcoming joint-venture offering involves eight fields, mostly in southern onshore Trinidad, but it also includes three near-shore blocks in the south of the island.
The country currently has 500 million barrels of proven oil reserves and 16.1 trillion cubic feet in proven gas deposits, but Baldeosingh said oil in place stood at two billion barrels.
Given Trinidad's massive gas reserves for such a small country, Baldeosingh was particularly looking for petrochemical proposals which use gas as a feedstock.

Trinidad has already begun construction of a $1 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant to produce three million tonnes per year. It is being built by Cabot, a consortium including Amoco and British Gas, and is due to come on line in May 1999.
Baldeosingh said already-agreed projects would make Trinidad the biggest exporter of methanol and ammonia in the world within a few years.
Upstream investment opportunities extended to developing Trinidad's heavy oil fields and tar sands, as neighbouring Venezuela is just beginning to do.

In the downstream sector, Petrotrin has just completed a $350 million upgrade of the Pointe-a-Pierre refinery, bringing capacity up to 160,000 bpd. Petrotrin was now on the hunt for partners in the plant, either for an equity stake or a crude supply deal, Baldeosingh said.
The plant was now able to produce unleaded gasoline and very low sulphur diesel, but Petrotrin wanted to see more units built to industrialise other refinery streams.

Trinidad's liberalisation was also spreading to oil retailing, where a phased liberalisation was due to start this year, Baldeosingh added. International companies would be allowed access from 1999 when prices are expected to move towards world levels, and full deregulation would follow in 2002.
Baldeosingh said Trinidad's success in attracting investment was due to its stable government, reliable judiciary, strategic location and lenient fiscal regime.
Foreign oil companies already produce two-thirds of the oil and nearly all Trinidad's gas, which currently stands at 700 million cubic feet per day.
